header: IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
body: KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO J. Through this single judgment, I intend to decide both the captioned writ petitions, as they involve the same parties and common questions of fact and law.

2. Through the instant writ petition filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, the Petitioner, Riaz Hanif Rahi, assails the impugned order dated 11.10.2025, passed by the learned Justice of Peace / Additional Sessions Judge (West), Islamabad (Respondent No.1), whereby the police stance was accepted. The application was disposed of without directing registration of an FIR.

3. Briefly, the facts giving rise to the instant petition are that the petitioner filed a complaint on 31.07.2025 under Tag No. 2091 before Respondent No.3, which remained unattended. The petitioner then sought remedy under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. before the learned Magistrate, who, on 11.08.2025, rejected the police report dated 08.08.2025 and directed action. Upon non-implementation, an enforcement application was moved; however, the police reiterated their stance. The learned Duty Magistrate, vide order dated 21.08.2025, rejected their stance, but the police recorded Rapt No.35 on the same day and dropped proceedings. The learned Magistrate probed into the matter, called for an ADR report on 25.08.2025, and on 27.08.2025 directed the S.H.O. to proceed strictly in accordance with law. The petitioner also filed a complaint under Section 155 of the Police Order, 2002 before Respondent No.4 (forwarded vide Diary No.443-CC), while a related application under Section 22-A(6)(iii) Cr.P.C. was disposed of on 15.09.2025. A show-cause notice was issued to the S.H.O. When the DSP submitted a report reiterating the same stance for the fourth time, the learned Magistrate on 19.09.2025 declared the report unreliable and ordered implementation. Thereafter, Respondent No.1 passed the impugned order dated 11.10.2025, adopting the police stance that was already rejected by the Magistrates.

4. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 2-A, 4, 9, and 25 of the Constitution have been infringed; that courts have no jurisdiction beyond the limits prescribed by law as held in Rawalpindi Bar Association v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2015 SC 401); that the investigative domain cannot be usurped by judges as held in Shahnaz Begum v. Honourable Judges (PLD 1971 SC 677) and Brig. (R) Imtiaz Ahmad v. Government of Pakistan (1994 SCMR 2142); that authoritative verdicts in PLD 2007 SC 539 and 2024 SCMR 1123 expressly restrain conducting inquiries prior to the registration of an FIR; that passing arbitrary findings without jurisdiction constitutes disrespect to the administration of justice and contempt under PLD 1994 SC 879; and that judicial functions are strictly confined to adjudicating controversies rather than assuming the role of an investigator or a party to the dispute.

5. In W.P. No.4205-2026, the Petitioner, Riaz Hanif Rahi, has assailed the order dated 11.10.2025, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge (West), Islamabad (Respondent No.1), whereby the criminal revision filed by Respondent No.2 was entertained, and administrative orders were treated as judicial orders.

6. Briefly, the facts giving rise to the instant petition are that the petitioner, who served as a legal consultant to Respondent No.2 (T & TECHS), raised a dispute regarding alterations made to an official fee/payment schedule letter dated 15.08.2024 and false allegations leveled against him. Upon filing a complaint dated 31.07.2025 (Tag No. 2091) before Respondent No.3 and subsequently invoking Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., the learned Area Magistrate passed administrative orders dated 03.09.2025 and 12.09.2025 against police inaction. Although no coercive direction had been issued against Respondent No. 2, its General Secretary filed a proxy Criminal Revision before Respondent No.1 at the Society’s expense, in violation of Rule 57(1)(a) of the Cooperative Societies Rules, 2018. The petitioner raised oral and written objections on 23.09.2025 and 25.09.2025 regarding the maintainability of the revision against administrative orders, relying upon Bahadur vs. The State (PLD 1985 SC 62). Meanwhile, following a newspaper report published in DAWN on 05.10.2025 regarding quo warranto proceedings against the District & Sessions Judge (W.P. No. 4044/2025), the learned Sessions Judge summoned the case files suo motu on 06.10.2025 without lawful authority. Ultimately, Respondent No.1 passed the impugned judgment dated 11.10.2025, disregarding binding precedent, treating administrative orders as judicial, and encroaching upon the investigative domain of the police.

7. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the fundamental rights under Articles 2-A, 4, 9, and 25 of the Constitution stand violated; that a criminal revision against administrative orders of a Magistrate is incompetent as held in Bahadur Vs. The State (PLD 1985 SC 62); that ignoring Supreme Court precedents amounts to contempt under PLD 1994 SC 879; that Respondent No.2 cannot file a criminal revision to defend individual office-bearers at society expense under Rule 57(1)(a) of Cooperative Societies Rules, 2018; that without challenging the foundational order dated 11.08.2025, the court could not travel beyond pleadings per PLD 1960 SC 1; and that Respondent No.1 unlawfully encroached upon executive police powers with mala fide intent.
8. Learned counsel for the respondents in W.P.

No.4206/2025 submits that the application under Section 22-A Cr.P.C. does not disclose any information constituting a cognizable offence; that the additional paragraph and the official professional bill presented by the petitioner were incorporated in the office copy; that the said additional paragraph does not constitute fraudulent incorporation, nor was it a condition that the professional fee would be paid to the petitioner after the conclusion of the trial. He, therefore, contends that the instant petition is liable to be dismissed.
9. Learned counsel for the respondents in W.P.

No.4205/2025 submits that the impugned order is not an administrative order, but a judicial order; that the case of Bahadur is not applicable to the facts of the present case; that detailed reasons have been recorded by the learned Additional Sessions Judge while allowing the revision petition; and that the impugned order does not call for interference by this Court. He, therefore, contends that the instant writ petition is liable to be dismissed.

10. I have heard the petitioner appearing in person, learned counsel for the respondent society and learned State Counsel, and have examined the available record in the light of the relevant statutory provisions and the law laid down by the superior Courts. Since both petitions arise out of the same proceedings, the questions requiring determination are, firstly, the scope of the powers exercisable by a Magistrate under Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., particularly in relation to registration of an FIR; secondly, whether the orders passed in exercise of such powers are administrative or judicial in character and amenable to criminal revision; and thirdly, whether the learned ex officio Justice of Peace lawfully exercised jurisdiction under Section 22-A(6), Cr.P.C.

11. The scheme of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, draws a distinction between registration of information, investigation of an offence and taking of cognizance by a Magistrate. Section 154, Cr.P.C., regulates the recording of information relating to a cognizable offence, whereas Section 156(1) authorizes the police to investigate such an offence without an order of the Magistrate. Subsection (3) of Section 156 empowers a Magistrate authorized under Section 190 to order such investigation. These provisions operate at different procedural stages and must be construed harmoniously so that each is given effect within its prescribed sphere.

12. The powers conferred under Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., are exercisable before the Magistrate takes cognizance of the matter as a private complaint. Where the information prima facie discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, the Magistrate may direct the concerned police officer to register a case and undertake investigation in accordance with law. However, once the Magistrate takes cognizance and examines the complainant under Section 200, Cr.P.C., the subsequent proceedings are governed by Chapter XVI, including Sections 202 to 204, Cr.P.C. This distinction was explained by the august Supreme Court in Muhammad Ramzan v. The State and others (1979 SCMR 200), wherein it was held that before taking cognizance the Magistrate may refer the matter to the police for registration and investigation, but having adopted the procedure prescribed for a private complaint, he cannot thereafter resort to Section 156(3), Cr.P.C. The same principle finds support in Raja Munawar Khan and others v. Muhammad Ishaque and another (PLD 1975 Lahore 577).

13. Although Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., expressly refers to ordering investigation, the power has been judicially interpreted as extending to registration of an FIR where such registration is necessary for investigation of a cognizable offence. The reliance in this regard may be made to Hazoor Bakhsh v. Senior Superintendent of Police, Rahim Yar Khan and others (PLD 1999 Lahore 417), Munir Ahmad v. The State and another (1990 P.Cr.L.J. 1547) and Muhammad Ali v. S.H.O., Police Station Aziz Bhatti and others (2003 YLR 550). Nevertheless, such power cannot be exercised mechanically. The Magistrate must consider whether the allegations disclose a cognizable offence and whether police investigation is warranted. A direction to proceed in accordance with law cannot invariably be construed as an unconditional command to register an FIR.

14. The jurisdiction of the Magistrate under Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., does not extend to determining the guilt of a nominated person or dictating the result of investigation. Once investigation is ordered, collection of evidence and formation of an investigative opinion remain within the statutory domain of the police. The august Supreme Court in Seeta Ram v. The State (2025 SCMR 2028) emphasized the obligation to record information concerning cognizable offences while recognizing the statutory limitations governing investigation and the supervisory functions of a Magistrate. Similarly, in F.I.A. through Director General, FIA and others v. Syed Hamid Ali Shah and others (PLD 2023 SC 265), the Supreme Court reiterated the distinction between cognizable and non-cognizable offences for purposes of registration and investigation. Thus, the authority to initiate the investigative process must not be confused with the authority to conduct or control its outcome.

15. The next question concerns the scope of criminal revisional jurisdiction. Sections 435 to 439-A, Cr.P.C., contemplate examination of proceedings before an inferior criminal Court for the purposes authorized by law. The mere fact that an order emanates from a Magistrate does not necessarily bring it within such jurisdiction. A Magistrate performs various functions under the Code, some judicial and others administrative, executive or ministerial. The nature of the particular function, rather than the designation of the officer exercising it, determines whether the resulting order forms part of a proceeding before a criminal Court.

16. The governing principle was authoritatively settled in Bahadur and another v. The State and another (PLD 1985 SC 62). In that case, the august Supreme Court examined whether an order passed by a Magistrate concurring with a police report under Section 173, Cr.P.C., and cancelling a registered criminal case was amenable to revision. The Supreme Court held that although the Magistrate was required to examine the report fairly and apply his mind, he was not functioning as a criminal Court while performing that particular duty. The Court distinguished judicial functions, which ordinarily involve determination of a controversy through a binding decision affecting rights, from administrative functions concerned with the regulation or supervision of public affairs. It was further observed that the requirement to act fairly, justly and honestly is not confined to judicial proceedings and does not, by itself, transform an administrative function into a judicial one.

17. An important feature of Bahadur's case is that the Supreme Court did not determine the character of the order merely from its form or the designation of the Magistrate. It examined whether there existed a lis requiring judicial determination, whether the parties were entitled to a hearing, whether a binding adjudication had been made and whether finality attached to the order. The Supreme Court found that concurrence with a police cancellation report did not finally determine the complainant's rights, since the complainant remained competent to institute a private complaint upon the same facts and the Magistrate did not become functus officio. Accordingly, such an order was held to be administrative in character and outside the revisional jurisdiction contemplated by Sections 435 to 439, Cr.P.C.

18. The ratio of Bahadur's case is that revisional jurisdiction cannot be invoked against every order requiring application of judicial mind. The distinction lies between acting judicially in the sense of exercising fairness and discretion, and acting as a criminal Court in the determination of a judicial proceeding. This principle must, however, be applied with reference to the particular statutory function under examination. Bahadur concerned cancellation of a police case upon a report under Section 173, Cr.P.C.; it did not lay down that every order passed under Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., is necessarily administrative or immune from judicial scrutiny. The nature, contents and legal effect of the particular order must therefore be independently assessed.

19. Reverting to W.P. No.4205/2025, the record reveals that Criminal Revision No.131/2025 was preferred against the Magistrate's orders dated 03.09.2025 and 12.09.2025. The learned revisional Court itself recorded that the earlier order contained no substantive observation and merely adjourned the proceedings, whereas the subsequent order concerned implementation of the directions previously issued to the police. Neither order, as described in the impugned judgment, appears to have determined the criminal liability of any person or finally adjudicated a dispute between the parties. Their substance related to the progress of proceedings concerning police action upon the petitioner's complaint.

20. The learned revisional Court nevertheless treated the orders as judicial in character without adequately examining the statutory capacity in which the Magistrate acted. The mere fact that the orders were passed in proceedings before a Magistrate, or that the Magistrate applied his mind while issuing directions, was insufficient to establish their revisability. Applying the principle enunciated in Bahadur's case, it was necessary to determine whether the Magistrate was exercising jurisdiction as a criminal Court or merely facilitating performance of the police functions contemplated by Section 156(3), Cr.P.C. In the absence of such determination, the assumption of revisional jurisdiction cannot be sustained merely upon the observation that the orders were judicial in nature.

21. The learned revisional Court further concluded that the police had complied with the earlier directions by recording Rapt No.35 dated 21.08.2025 and treating the controversy as civil. It consequently held that no further proceedings before the Magistrate were required. However, the sufficiency of the police response could not independently confer revisional jurisdiction where the challenged orders were not otherwise amenable to revision. Jurisdiction must be established before the merits are examined; it cannot be derived from the conclusion that the proceedings before the Magistrate ought to have been discontinued.

22. It is also relevant that the original direction dated 11.08.2025 was not itself the subject of the criminal revision. The subsequent orders arose in the course of proceedings concerning implementation of that direction. Although the failure to challenge the original order does not, by itself, determine the maintainability of revision against a subsequent order, the revisional Court was required to remain within the jurisdiction lawfully attracted by the orders actually challenged. It could not enlarge the scope of revision merely to pronounce upon the adequacy of the police investigation or the desirability of continuing proceedings before the Magistrate.

23. In the circumstances, the learned revisional Court failed to identify a legally sustainable basis for exercising revisional jurisdiction over the orders under challenge. Its conclusion that the orders were judicial in character was not supported by the examination required under the principle laid down in Bahadur's case. Consequently, the impugned judgment dated 11.10.2025, passed in Criminal Revision No.131/2025, is liable to be set aside, without expressing any opinion regarding the truthfulness of the allegations made by the petitioner or the necessity of registering an FIR.

24. Having examined the statutory framework and the principles enunciated by the superior Courts, this Court now proceeds to consider the legality of the judgment dated 11.10.2025 passed by the learned Additional District and Sessions Judge (West), Islamabad, in Criminal Revision No.131/2025. The primary question is whether the orders dated 03.09.2025 and 12.09.2025, passed by the learned Magistrate during proceedings arising under Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., constituted judicial orders amenable to revisional jurisdiction, or whether they merely regulated the performance of investigative functions by the police. The distinction is of fundamental importance because revisional jurisdiction is a creation of statute and cannot be exercised merely on the ground that an order passed by a Magistrate is considered erroneous or inconvenient by an affected person.

25. A perusal of the impugned judgment reveals that the learned revisional Court itself recorded in paragraph 6 that the order dated 03.09.2025 contained no material observation and that the matter was merely adjourned for further proceedings. It was further observed that the subsequent order dated 12.09.2025 required the concerned S.H.O. to implement the earlier direction dated 11.08.2025, whereby the police had been directed to proceed in accordance with law if the alleged offence was found to have been made out. Thus, even according to the findings recorded by the learned revisional Court, neither of the challenged orders amounted to a final adjudication of the criminal liability of any person. The proceedings remained concerned with the response of the police to the petitioner's complaint and compliance with the directions issued in that regard.

26. Reverting to the facts of the present case, the controversy essentially emanates from an arrangement concerning professional legal services rendered by the petitioner to the respondent cooperative housing society. According to the petitioner, he was entitled to consideration in the shape of allotment of a plot measuring 30 x 60 feet or payment of its alternative value, whereas the subsequent arrangement allegedly contemplated payment of Rs.5,000,000/-, against which an amount of Rs.300,000/was paid. The petitioner's grievance primarily concerns the nonpayment of his professional fees and the alleged alteration of a letter dated 15.08.2024. The question requiring consideration is whether these allegations, when taken at their face value, disclose the commission of a cognizable offence or merely reflect a disagreement concerning the terms and enforcement of a professional engagement.

27. During the course of arguments, learned counsel representing the proposed accused produced before this Court a copy of the letter dated 15.08.2024 and explained that the document was merely an office copy containing a proposed term incorporated in handwriting. It was submitted that the handwritten portion contemplated only that the petitioner, as counsel for the respondent society, would receive his professional fees after the conclusion of the cases entrusted to him. A perusal of the disputed portion reveals that it relates exclusively to when the professional fees would become payable. The incorporation of such a condition, by itself, neither establishes fabrication of a document nor necessarily constitutes its fraudulent alteration. The mere existence of a handwritten insertion in an office copy cannot, without more, be equated with forgery or tampering in the criminal sense.

28. It is equally significant that the disputed handwritten portion neither purports to extinguish the petitioner's entitlement to professional fees nor introduces any allegation of impersonation, fabrication of signatures or creation of a false document. Its apparent effect is confined to prescribing the time for payment of the professional consideration, namely, after conclusion of the cases. Whether such a condition formed part of the agreement between the parties, or was subsequently introduced without the petitioner's consent, may raise a dispute about the terms and enforceability of the professional engagement. However, the mere incorporation of a proposed term regarding the time of payment, without facts constituting the essential ingredients of a penal offence, cannot automatically be characterized as criminal forgery. A contractual disagreement does not acquire criminal character merely because one party describes an insertion as tampering.

29. The distinction assumes importance because criminal liability for forgery or the use of a forged document requires the existence of the essential statutory ingredients of the relevant offence. Mere alteration of the appearance or wording of a document is not sufficient in every case. The nature of the alteration, the authority under which it was made, its intended use and the dishonest or fraudulent purpose alleged are material considerations. In the present matter, the petitioner relies on the handwritten incorporation, as explained during arguments, which concerns the time of payment of professional fees. The allegations do not, on their face, sufficiently disclose that a false document was made or dishonestly used in the manner contemplated by the penal law. Consequently, the disputed insertion, lacking the requisite criminal ingredients, cannot independently provide a lawful basis to direct the registration of an FIR.

30. The principles laid down by the august Supreme Court in Muhammad Bashir v. Station House Officer, Okara Cantt. and others (PLD 2007 SC 539) and Syed Qamber Ali Shah v. Province of Sindh and others (2024 SCMR 1123) leave no room for doubt that where information discloses a cognizable offence, its registration cannot be refused upon an assessment of the truthfulness or otherwise of the allegations. However, these authorities do not dispense with the fundamental requirement that the information must, in the first instance, disclose the commission of a cognizable offence. The learned Justice of the Peace is not required to direct registration of an FIR merely upon the use of expressions such as fraud, forgery or tampering, unless the factual allegations disclose conduct falling within the ingredients of a cognizable offence. The distinction between examining whether an offence is disclosed and inquiring whether the offence has actually been committed must be carefully maintained.

31. Examined against this legal framework, the petitioner's grievance essentially concerns recovery of professional fees and disagreement over the stage at which such fees became payable. The handwritten portion of the office copy, which provides for payment upon conclusion of the cases, does not, merely because it was incorporated by hand, disclose the commission of a cognizable offence. Even if the petitioner disputes the incorporation of that condition, such disagreement, in the absence of allegations satisfying the essential ingredients of forgery or another cognizable offence, is a matter concerning the respective contractual rights and obligations of the parties. The machinery of criminal law cannot be invoked merely to secure performance of a disputed contractual commitment or recovery of professional remuneration.

32. There is yet another aspect of the matter which cannot escape judicial consideration. The petitioner has placed considerable reliance upon the orders previously passed by the learned Magistrate under Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., particularly the directions requiring the police to proceed in accordance with law. However, the legal effect of such directions must be examined within the limits of the statutory jurisdiction under which they were issued. Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., empowers a Magistrate to order investigation as contemplated under Section 156(1), Cr.P.C., and does not authorize an inquiry to ascertain the truthfulness of allegations before registration of a cognizable case. Thus, the statutory function of the Magistrate cannot be extended to conducting or authorizing a preliminary inquiry in substitution for the procedure prescribed by Section 154, Cr.P.C. Equally, a direction to proceed in accordance with law cannot be construed as an unconditional command to register an FIR irrespective of whether the information discloses a cognizable offence. The requirement that the information must disclose a cognizable offence remains fundamental to the operation of Section 154, Cr.P.C.

33. Applying the aforesaid principle to the present case, the successive orders passed by the learned Magistrate requiring implementation of the earlier directions could neither enlarge the statutory powers of the police nor dispense with the requirement that the allegations must disclose a cognizable offence. The mere rejection of a police report or insistence upon compliance with an earlier order could not transform an essentially contractual dispute into a criminal case. The learned ex officio Justice of Peace was therefore required to examine the information independently within the limited jurisdiction conferred by Section 22-A(6), Cr.P.C. As held by the august Supreme Court in Muhammad Bashir v. Station House Officer, Okara Cantt. and others (PLD 2007 SC 539), subsequently reaffirmed in Syed Qamber Ali Shah v. Province of Sindh and others (2024 SCMR 1123), the relevant inquiry at that stage is confined to whether the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. The Justice of Peace cannot determine the truthfulness of the allegations through an elaborate inquiry, nor is he bound to order registration merely because an applicant alleges fraud or forgery without narrating facts constituting the essential ingredients of such an offence.

34. In the present case, the controversy concerning the professional fees of the petitioner and the handwritten incorporation in the office copy of the letter dated 15.08.2024, when examined in the manner prescribed by the aforesaid authorities, does not disclose the necessary ingredients of a cognizable offence. During arguments, learned counsel for the proposed accused produced a copy of the disputed letter and explained that the handwritten portion was incorporated in the office copy as a proposed term regarding payment of professional fees after conclusion of the cases. The allegation regarding such incorporation, even when considered independently of the explanation furnished by learned counsel, essentially relates to the time at which the professional fees were to become payable. No sufficient factual foundation has been disclosed to show that the handwritten insertion, merely by reason of its existence, constituted the making or fraudulent use of a false document. The dispute therefore remains one concerning the terms and enforcement of a professional engagement. In these circumstances, the refusal of the learned Justice of Peace to direct registration of an FIR does not suffer from any jurisdictional defect warranting interference under Article 199 of the Constitution.

35. As regards the connected W.P. No.4205/2025, the question of revisional jurisdiction must be determined independently of the merits of the underlying allegations. The august Supreme Court in Bahadur and another v. The State and another (PLD 1985 SC 62) explained that every order passed by a Magistrate does not necessarily constitute a judicial order amenable to criminal revision. The decisive consideration is the nature of the function exercised and whether the Magistrate was acting as a criminal Court in the determination of a judicial proceeding. Although the said judgment concerned cancellation of a criminal case upon acceptance of a police report under Section 173, Cr.P.C., the distinction drawn therein between judicial and administrative functions is relevant to the present controversy. The orders dated 03.09.2025 and 12.09.2025, as described in the impugned revisional judgment, did not determine any lis or finally adjudicate the rights of the parties. The former merely adjourned the proceedings, whereas the latter concerned compliance with earlier directions relating to police action. Their substance was therefore supervisory rather than adjudicatory. The learned revisional Court, without examining this distinction, proceeded to exercise revisional jurisdiction and interfere with those orders. Such assumption of jurisdiction was inconsistent with the principle laid down in Bahadur's case.

36. It is also important to observe that the question whether the petitioner's application disclosed a cognizable offence and the question whether the Magistrate's orders were amenable to criminal revision are legally distinct. An order passed without revisional jurisdiction cannot be sustained merely because the conclusion reached therein may otherwise be legally correct. Conversely, setting aside an order passed in excess of revisional jurisdiction does not necessarily establish the petitioner's entitlement to registration of an FIR. The former question concerns the lawful exercise of jurisdiction, whereas the latter concerns the existence of the statutory conditions contemplated by Section 154, Cr.P.C. Both questions must be determined independently in accordance with their respective governing principles.

37. In view of the foregoing discussion, W.P. No.4206/2025 is DISMISSED, as the information supplied by the petitioner, examined on its face value, does not disclose the necessary ingredients of a cognizable offence warranting directions for registration of an FIR under Section 22-A(6), Cr.P.C. However, W.P. No.4205/2025 is ALLOWED and the impugned revisional order dated 11.10.2025, passed in Crl. Revision No.131/2025, is SET-ASIDE for want of lawful exercise of revisional jurisdiction. The orders previously passed by the learned Magistrate under Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., shall not be construed as unconditional directions for registration of an FIR, nor shall the setting aside of the revisional order be understood as reviving any direction inconsistent with the statutory scheme explained above. The petitioner shall, however, remain at liberty to pursue such remedy as may be available under the law for enforcement of his contractual rights.
(KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO)
JUDGE Announced in open Court on 11.11.2026.
JUDGE RAMZAN APPROVED FOR REPROTING.
